The transaction locks the selected row, reads 5, reduces it to 3, and commits. This one-session example illustrates the sequence; it does not prove concurrent behavior. Use a shared disposable table and two sessions for a real lock test, since temporary tables are session-local.

The transaction temporarily changes book 1 to zero. ROLLBACK cancels that change, so the final SELECT returns 100. Replacing ROLLBACK with COMMIT would keep zero. Test both on fresh copies; a successful rollback does not prove that a separate backup can be restored.

The tree separates task behavior, local storage, and reusable fields. It is a design sketch, not a runnable project. A reducer should be testable without rendering React. The update changes the title of row 1 only. Its id stays 1, so references remain meaningful. Without WHERE, every title would change. In a fresh practice copy, try inserting another row with id 1 and expect a key constraint failure rather than two ambiguous identities.

The validator rejects empty and whitespace-only names. The test passes an empty string and expects false. It does not test the whole screen or packaging. Add a whitespace case, a real name, and an interaction test verifying that an invalid form keeps its input and shows a useful message.

There are two price groups. Price 100 has two rows and price 150 has one. COUNT(*) counts rows, not the numeric sum of prices. SUM(price) across the original table is 350. An empty input makes SUM return NULL, so choose an explicit empty-total policy.
